items.prompt: What does a Bloom filter give up to answer membership questions in a few bits per item?

options.text: Speed: queries get slower as it fills
options.rationale: A query always checks exactly k bits, so its cost does not grow.

options.text: Exactness: it can sometimes say yes to an item it never saw
options.rationale: Correct. It trades a small rate of false positives for fixed, small memory (Section 1).

options.text: The ability to say no
options.rationale: It says no with certainty; that is its strong answer.

options.text: Nothing; it is an exact set in fewer bits
options.rationale: No structure can store arbitrary items exactly in a few bits each.

items.prompt: Why does an exact set use more memory as items get longer, while a Bloom filter does not?

required.idea: An exact set stores the items themselves
A Bloom filter stores only bits set by hashes

misconceptions.description: Thinks a Bloom filter stores the items

items.modelAnswer: An exact set has to keep every item, so long items cost more. A Bloom filter keeps only a fixed array of bits that hashes point into, so the length of an item does not matter.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend what problem a Bloom filter solves and what it trades away.

required.idea: It answers whether an item has been seen before
It uses little, fixed memory
It can give false positives

items.modelAnswer: It answers 'have I seen this before?' using a few bits per item instead of storing the items. The price is that it can occasionally say yes to something it never saw.

items.prompt: You hash the string "apple" twice with the same function. What do you get?

options.text: The same number both times
options.rationale: Correct. Hash functions are deterministic, which is why a query finds the bits an insert set.

options.text: Two different random numbers
options.rationale: Then a query could never find the bits the insert set.

options.text: It depends on the time of day
options.rationale: Hashes do not depend on time.

options.text: The string itself
options.rationale: A hash is a number derived from the input, not the input.

items.prompt: With double hashing, h1 = 10, h2 = 7 and m = 16. What is the position for i = 3, that is (h1 + 3 * h2) mod 16?
Explain to a friend what a Bloom filter needs from its hash functions, and how double hashing gets k positions from two hashes.

required.idea: The same input always gives the same output
Outputs spread evenly
Position i is (h1 + i * h2) mod m

items.modelAnswer: Each hash must give the same number for the same input and spread different inputs evenly. Instead of k separate functions, compute two hashes h1 and h2 and use (h1 + i * h2) mod m for i from 0 to k - 1.

items.prompt: A query finds one of the item's k bits set to 0. What can you conclude?

options.text: The item was definitely never inserted
options.rationale: Correct. Inserting it would have set that bit to 1, and bits are never cleared.

options.text: The item was probably inserted
options.rationale: That is the answer when all k bits are 1.

options.text: Nothing; you need to check the other bits
options.rationale: One zero is enough: an inserted item has all k bits set.

options.text: The filter is corrupted
options.rationale: Most queries for absent items find a zero; that is normal.

items.prompt: A new filter has m = 64 bits and k = 3. You insert one item whose three positions are all different. How many bits are now 1?
items.explanation: One insert sets k bits; with no overlaps that is 3.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend how insert and query work, and why a Bloom filter never gives a false negative.

required.idea: Insert sets the item's k bits to 1
Query checks the same k bits
Inserted items always find their bits set, so no false negatives

misconceptions.description: Thinks the filter can miss an inserted item

items.modelAnswer: To insert, hash the item k times and set those bits to 1. To query, hash it the same way and check those bits: any 0 means definitely not inserted, all 1 means probably inserted. Bits are never cleared, so an inserted item always finds its bits set: no false negatives.

items.prompt: Rebuild the bit array (exercise 01-bit-array).
Rebuild insert and query (exercise 02-bloom-filter).
m = 1000 bits, n = 100 items, k = 7. Using p = (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, what is the false-positive rate? Give a decimal to 4 places.
You keep inserting items into a fixed-size filter. What happens to the false-positive rate?

options.text: It stays the same
options.rationale: More inserts set more bits, so absent items find all their bits set more often.

options.text: It rises
options.rationale: Correct. The rate depends on kn/m, which grows with n.

options.text: It falls
options.rationale: Fuller filters make accidental matches more likely, not less.

options.text: It rises until half full, then falls
options.rationale: It keeps rising; a full filter says yes to everything.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend where false positives come from and why they get more common as the filter fills.

required.idea: Other items set all k bits by chance
More inserts mean more bits set to 1

items.modelAnswer: A false positive happens when other items have, between them, set every one of the k bits a new item checks. Each insert sets more bits to 1, so the fuller the filter, the more likely that is.

items.prompt: Capstone: compute and measure false-positive rates (exercise 03-sizing).
m = 1000 bits and n = 100 items. What whole number k minimises the false-positive rate, using k = (m/n) ln 2?
Why does adding more hash functions eventually make the false-positive rate worse?

options.text: Hashing gets slower
options.rationale: Speed is a separate cost; the question is about the rate.

options.text: Each insert sets more bits, so the filter fills faster
options.rationale: Correct. Past k = (m/n) ln 2 the extra bits set outweigh the extra bits checked.

options.text: Hash functions start to collide with each other
options.rationale: Collisions are part of the model already; the problem is the filling.

options.text: It does not; more hashes always help
options.rationale: The rate has a minimum at k = (m/n) ln 2.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend how to size a Bloom filter for a target false-positive rate, including the 1% rule of thumb.

required.idea: m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2
About 9.6 bits per item for 1%
Then k = (m/n) ln 2

misconceptions.description: Thinks more hash functions always help
synonyms: more hash functions is always better

items.modelAnswer: Pick n and the rate p you can live with, then use m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits: about 9.6 bits per item for 1%. Then choose k = (m/n) ln 2, which leaves about half the bits set.

items.prompt: Capstone: size a filter and check it against a real one (exercise 03-sizing).
Why can you not delete an item from a plain Bloom filter by clearing its k bits?

options.text: Clearing bits is slow
options.rationale: Clearing a bit is as fast as setting one.

options.text: Other items may share those bits, and would then be missed
options.rationale: Correct. That would create false negatives, which the filter promises never to give (Section 6).

options.text: Bits can only be set once by hardware
options.rationale: The array is ordinary memory.

options.text: You can; it works fine
options.rationale: It breaks other items that share a bit.

items.prompt: How does a counting Bloom filter support deletion, and what does it cost?

required.idea: Each position holds a counter instead of a bit
Insert increments and delete decrements
It needs more memory

items.modelAnswer: It stores a small counter at each position. Inserting increments the k counters and deleting decrements them, so shared positions stay non-zero. It costs several times more memory.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend why deleting from a Bloom filter is a problem and how counting filters fix it.

required.idea: Bits are shared between items
Clearing them would cause false negatives
Counters instead of bits allow decrementing

misconceptions.description: Thinks deleting means clearing the bits

items.modelAnswer: Several items can share a bit, so clearing one item's bits can wipe out bits other items need, and they would start getting 'definitely not': false negatives. A counting filter keeps a counter per position, so delete can decrement without erasing other items.
